section.title: Introduction
section.para: tac_plus-ng is a TACACS+ daemon that supports RADIUS, too. It provides networking components like routers and switches with authentication, authorisation and accounting services.
This version is a major rewrite of the original public Cisco source code and is in turn largely based on tac_plus, which comes with the same distribution. Key features include:

listitem.para: NAS specific device keys, prompts, enable passwords
Rule-based permission assignment
Flexible external back-ends for user profiles (e.g. via PERL scripts or C; LDAP (including ActiveDirectory), RADIUS and others are included)
Connection multiplexing (multiple concurrent NAS clients per process)
Session multiplexing (multiple concurrent sessions per connection, single-connection)
Scalable, no limit on users, clients or servers.
CLI context aware.
Full support for both IPv4 and IPv6
Implements and auto-detects HAProxy protocol 2.
Supports TACACS+ over TLS1.3
Compliant to RFC8907
Supports Linux VRFs
Supports (non-standard) SSH Public Key Authentication (see the Wiki for reference)
Implements and auto-detects legacy RADIUS (UDP and TCP), RADSEC (TLS) and RADIUS/DTLS (with PAP, CHAP, MSCHAPv1 and MSCHAPv2 authentication).
Supports RADIUS Downloadable ACLs.

section.title: Download
section.para: You can download the source code from the GitHub repository at https://github.com/tacplus-ng/event-driven-servers/. On-line documentation is available via https://tacplus-ng.github.io/event-driven-servers/doc/index.html, too.

section.title: Definitions and Terms
section.para: The following chapters utilize a couple of terms that may need further explanation:

row.entry: A Network Access Client, e.g. the source device of a ssh (or telnet) connection.
A Network Access Server or Device, e.g. a Cisco box, or any other client which makes TACACS+ or RADIUS requests or generates accounting packets.
A program which services network requests for authentication and authorization, verifies identities, grants or denies authorizations, and logs accounting records.
Strings of text in the form attribute=value, sent between a NAS and a TACACS+ daemon as part of the TACACS+ protocol.

section.para: Since a NAS is sometimes referred to as a server, and a daemon is also often referred to as a server, the term server has been avoided here in favor of the less ambiguous terms NAS and Daemon.

section.title: Operation
section.para: This section gives a brief and basic overview on how to run tac_plus-ng.

In earlier versions, tac_plus wasn't a standalone program but had to be invoked by spawnd. This has changed, as spawnd functionality is now part of the tac_plus binary. However, using a dedicated spawnd process is still possible and, more importantly, the spawnd configuration options and documentation remain valid.
tac_plus-ng may use auxiliary MAVIS back-end modules for authentication of users and authorization of users and hosts.

section.title: Command line syntax
section.para: The only mandatory argument is the path to the configuration file:
section.screen: tac_plus-ng [ -P ] [ -d level ] [ -i child_id ] configuration-file [ id ]
section.para: If the program was compiled with CURL support, configuration-file may be an URL.
Keep the -P option in mind - it is imperative that the configuration file supplied is syntactically correct, as the daemon won't start if there are any parsing errors.
The -d switch enables debugging. You most likely don't want to use this. Read the source if you need to.

The -i option is only honoured if the build-in spawnd functionality is used. In that case, it selects the configuration ID for tac_plus, while the optional last argument id sets the ID of the spawnd configuration section.

section.title: Signals
section.para: Both the master (that's the process running the spawnd code) and the child processes (running the tac_plus-ng code) intercept the SIGHUP signal:

listitem.para: The master process will restart upon reception of SIGHUP, re-reading the configuration file. The child processes will recognize that the master process is no longer available. It will continue to serve the existing connections and terminate when idle.
If SIGHUP is sent to a child process it will stop accepting new connections from its master process. It will continue to serve the existing connections and terminate when idle.

section.para: Sending SIGUSR1 to the master process will cause it to abandon existing child processes (these will continue to serve the existing connections only) and start new child processes.

section.title: Event mechanism selection
section.para: Several level-triggered event mechanisms are supported. By default, the one best suited for your operating system will be used. However, you may set the environment variable IO_POLL_MECHANISM to select a specific one.
The following event mechanisms are supported (in order of preference):

listitem.para: port (Sun Solaris 10 and higher only, IO_POLL_MECHANISM=32)
kqueue (*BSD and Darwin only, IO_POLL_MECHANISM=1)
/dev/poll (Sun Solaris only, IO_POLL_MECHANISM=2)
epoll (Linux only, IO_POLL_MECHANISM=4)
poll (IO_POLL_MECHANISM=8)
select (IO_POLL_MECHANISM=16)

section.para: Environment variables can be set in the configuration file at top-level:
section.screen: setenv IO_POLL_MECHANISM = 4

section.title: Realms
section.para: Bascially, realms are containers to logically separate configuration sets. At top-level, there's the default realm (called default internally). Realms pass on most configurations (e.g. logging, users (if there are no users defined in that realm scope), groups, profiles) to their sub-realms.
Realm selection is intially based on spawnd configuration:
If VRFs are used and no realm is specified in the spawnd section, the daemon will try to use the VRF name as realm and fall back to the default realm if that "vrf realm" isn't defined.
A realm can be selected based on device address, too:
section.screen: device myDevices { address = 10.1.23.0/24 target-realm = realmOne }

section.screen: realm realmName { ... }

section.title: Spoofing Syslog Packets
section.para: The script tacspooflog-ng.pl (which comes bundled with this distribution, have a look at the tac_plus-ng/extra/ directory) may be used to make syslogd believe that logs come straight from your router, not from tac_plus-ng.
E.g., if your syslogd is listening on 127.0.0.1, you may try:
section.screen: access log = "|exec sudo /path/to/tacspooflog-ng.pl 127.0.0.1"
section.para: This may be useful if you want to keep logs in a common place.
In contrast to the older tacspooflog.pl script tacspooflog-ng.pl will handle both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and has more configuration options.
Please read tac_plus-ng/extra/tacspooflog-ng.README too, if you're thinking about using this script.

caution.para: As soon as you issue this command, you will no longer be able to create new logins to your NAS without a functioning TACACS+ daemon appropriately configured with usernames and password, so make sure you have this ready.

As a safety measure while setting up, you should configure an enable secret and make it the last resort authentication method, so if your TACACS+ daemon fails to respond you will be able to use the NAS enable password to login. To do this, configure:
caution.screen: aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ enable
caution.para: or, to if you have local accounts:
caution.screen: aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
caution.para: If all else fails, and you find yourself locked out of the NAS due to a configuration problem, the section on recovering from lost passwords on Cisco's CCO web page will help you dig your way out.

section.title: Configuring Authorization
section.para: Authorization must be configured on both the NAS and the daemon to operate correctly. By default, the NAS will allow everything until you configure it to make authorization requests to the daemon.
On the daemon, the opposite is true: The daemon will, by default, deny authorization of anything that isn't explicitly permitted.

Authorization allows the daemon to deny commands and services outright, or to modify commands and services on a per-user basis. Authorization on the daemon is divided into two separate parts: commands and services.

section.title: Authorizing Commands
section.para: Exec commands are those commands which are typed at a NAS exec prompt. When authorization is requested by the NAS, the entire command is sent to the tac_plus daemon for authorization.
Command authorization is configured by telling the ruleset to apply a profile to the user. See the Profile section for details.

section.title: The Authorization Process
section.para: Authorizing a single session can result in multiple requests being sent to the daemon. For example, in order to authorize a dialin PPP user for IP, the following authorization requests will be made from the NAS:

listitem.para: An initial authorization request to startup PPP from the exec, using the AV pairs service=ppp, protocol=ip, will be made (Note: this initial request will be omitted if you are autoselecting PPP, since you won't know the username yet).

This request is really done to find the address for dumb PPP (or SLIP) clients who can't do address negotiation. Instead, they expect you to tell them what address to use before PPP starts up, via a text message e.g. "Entering PPP. Your address is 1.2.3.4". They rely on parsing this address from the message to know their address.

Next, an authorization request is made from the PPP subsystem to see if PPP's LCP layer is authorized. LCP parameters can be set at this time (e.g. callback). This request contains the AV pairs service=ppp, protocol=lcp.
Next an authorization request to startup PPP's IPCP layer is made using the AV pairs service=ppp, protocol=ipcp. Any parameters returned by the daemon are cached.

Next, during PPP's address negotiation phase, each time the remote peer requests a specific address, if that address isn't in the cache obtained in step 3, a new authorization request is made to see if the peers requested address is allowable. This step can be repeated multiple times until both sides agree on the remote peer's address or until the NAS (or client) decide they're never going to agree and they shut down PPP instead.

section.title: Authorization Relies on Authentication
section.para: Since we pretty much rely on having a username in authorization requests to decide which addresses etc. to hand out, it is important to know where the username for a PPP user comes from. There are generally 2 possible sources:

listitem.para: You force the user to authenticate by making her login to the exec and you use that login name in authorization requests. This username isn't propagated to PPP by default. To have this happen, you generally need to configure the if-needed method, e.g.
listitem.screen: aaa authentication login default tacacs+ aaa authentication ppp default if-needed

listitem.para: Alternatively, you can run an authentication protocol, PAP or CHAP (CHAP is much preferred), to identify the user. You don't need an explicit login step if you do this (so it's the only possibility if you are using autoselect). This authentication gets done before you see the first LCP authorization request of course. Typically you configure this by doing:
listitem.screen: aaa authentication ppp default tacacs+ int async 1 ppp authentication chap

section.para: If you omit either of these authentication schemes, you will start to see authorization requests in which the username is missing.

section.title: Configuring Service Authorization
section.para: A list of AV pairs is placed in the daemon's configuration file in order to authorize services. The daemon compares each NAS AV pair to its configured AV pairs and either allows or denies the service. If the service is allowed, the daemon may add, change or delete AV pairs before returning them to the NAS, thereby restricting what the user is permitted to do.

section.title: The Authorization Algorithm
section.para: The complete algorithm by which the daemon processes its configured AV pairs against the list the NAS sends, is given below.
Find the user (or group) entry for this service (and protocol), then for each AV pair sent from the NAS:

listitem.para: If the AV pair from the NAS is mandatory:
look for an exact attribute,value match in the user's mandatory list. If found, add the AV pair to the output.
If an exact match doesn't exist, look in the user's optional list for the first attribute match. If found, add the NAS AV pair to the output.
If no attribute match exists, deny the command if the default is to deny, or,
If the default is permit, add the NAS AV pair to the output.
If the AV pair from the NAS is optional:
look for an exact attribute,value match in the user's mandatory list. If found, add DAEMON's AV pair to output.
If not found, look for the first attribute match in the user's mandatory list. If found, add DAEMON's AV pair to output.
If no mandatory match exists, look for an exact attribute,value pair match among the daemon's optional AV pairs. If found add the DAEMON's matching AV pair to the output.
If no exact match exists, locate the first attribute match among the daemon's optional AV pairs. If found add the DAEMON's matching AV pair to the output.
If no match is found, delete the AV pair if the default is deny, or
If the default is permit add the NAS AV pair to the output.

After all AV pairs have been processed, for each mandatory DAEMON AV pair, if there is no attribute match already in the output list, add the AV pair (but add only ONE AV pair for each mandatory attribute).

After all AV pairs have been processed, for each optional unrequested DAEMON AV pair, if there is no attribute match already in the output list, add that AV pair (but add only ONE AV pair for each optional attribute).

You should really have a look at the MAVIS documentation. It gives examples for RADIUS and PAM authentication, too.

section.title: Shadow Backend
section.para: mavis_tacplus_shadow.pl may be used to keep user passwords out of the tac_plusconfiguration file, enabling users to change their passwords via the password change dialog. Passwords are stored in an auxiliary, /etc/shadow-like ASCII file, one user per line:
section.screen: username:encryptedPassword:lastChange:minAge:maxAge:reserved
section.para: lastChange is the number of days since 1970-01-01 when the password was last changed, and minAge and maxAge determine whether the password may/may not/needs to be changed. Setting lastChange to 0 enforces a password change upon first login.
Example shadow file:

section.title: RADIUS Backends
section.para: mavis_tacplus_radius.pl authenticates against a RADIUS server. No authorization is done, unless the RADIUS_GROUP_ATTR environment variable is set (see below). This module may, for example, be useful if you have static user account definitions in the configuration file, but authentication passwords should be verified by RADIUS. Use the login = mavis or password = mavis statement in the user profile for this to work.

If the Authen::Radius Perl module is installed, the value of the RADIUS attribute specified by RADIUS_GROUP_ATTR will be used to create a TAC_MEMBER definition which uses the attribute value as group membership. E.g., an attribute value of Administrator would result in a
section.screen: member = Administrator
section.para: declaration for the authenticated user, enabling authorization and omitting the need for static users in the configuration file.
Keep in mind that authorization will only work well if either

mavis cache timeout is set to a sufficiently high value that covers the user's (expected) maximum login time.

section.title: Error Handling
section.para: If a back-end script fails due to an external problem (e.g. LDAP server unavailability), your router may or may not fall back to local authentication (if configured). Chances are that the fallback doesn't work. If you still want to be able to authenticate via TACACS+ in that case, you can do so with a non-MAVIS user which will only be valid in case of a back-end error:
section.screen: ... # set the time interval you want the user to be valid if the back-end fails: authentication fallback period = 60 # that's actually the default value ... # add a local user for emergencies: user = cisco { ... fallback-only ... }
section.para: To indicate that fallback mode is actually active, you may a display a different login prompt to your users:
Fallback can be enabled/disabled globally an on a per-device basis. Default is enabled.
Backend failures are detected per-process. However, you can sync fallback state between worker processes via the file system, on a per-realm basis:
section.screen: authentication fallback file = /tmp/tac/my_realm/fallack

section.title: RADIUS
section.para: tac_plus-ng comes with RADIUS support: PAP/CHAP/MSCHAPv1/MSCHAPv2 authentications, accounting and Downloadable ACLs are supported. This should be sufficient for handling administrative access, and it obviously provides a common configuration for both TACACS+ and RADIUS

If you don't care about RADIUS: That functionality will not be available unless a RADIUS dictionary (see below) is configured, and TLS/DTLS/Message-Signing absolutely requires building with OpenSSL support.
Also, you can selectively disable the protocols you want to be supported on a per-realm basis:
section.screen: aaa.protocol.allowed = tacacs,tacacs.tcp,tacacs.tls,radius,radius.udp,radius.tls,radius.dtls # Actually "tacacs" covers both "tacacs.tcp" (plain TACACS+) and "tacacs.tls" (Secure TACACS+"). # Likewise, "radius" covers RADIUS, RADIUS-TCP, RADSEC and RADIUS-DTLS.

section.title: Accepting RADIUS Queries
section.para: By default, spawnd will only care for TCP sessions. This is sufficient for RADIUS-over-TLS (RADSEC), but plain legacy RADIUS requires UDP. This can easily be enables in a spawnd directive:

In fact, the daemon auto-recognizes the supported protocols. You can use the very same TCP port for TACACS+, TACACS+-over-TLS and RADSEC-over-TLS, and the UDP port(s) specified for RADIUS will accept both authentication and accounting packets. However, defining the secondary port (with the accounting flag enabled is required for correct handling of RADIUS Server-Status requests.
UDP RADIUS sessions will be accepted only if a matching key (shared secret) exits. You can define that in host context:
section.screen: radius.key = mysecretkey
section.para: RADSEC doesn't need this key definition.

section.title: RADIUS DACLs
section.para: CISCO downloadable ACLs (dACLs, DACLs) are supported for RADIUS. Downloadable ACL sample definition:
section.screen: dacl demoacl { # prefix = "ip:inacl" # This is the default. # version = 12345678 # This is explained somewhere below. data = " deny ip host 10.0.0.0 any permit ip any any " }
section.para: In user profile context, you can then
section.screen: set radius[Cisco:Cisco-AVPair] = "ACS:CiscoSecure-Defined-ACL=${dacl:demoacl}"
section.para: which will instruct the device to query for that ACL via RADIUS.

The device will see the demoacl portion as something like #ACSACL#demoacl-00bc614e, where the suffix is, in hexadecimal, either the manually set version number (version = 12345678, that is 0x00bc614e) or the first 4 bytes of the ACL MD5 checksum. The version is always printed as 8 hex digits, never in decimal.
MAVIS support is there, too. One of the demo scripts (mavis_tacplus-ng-demo-database.pl) shows how to handle that.
No syntax checking is done for the data argument. If you mess up on that then the device will likely reject the connection.

section.title: RADIUS EAP-TLS
section.para: tac_plus-ng can terminate EAP-TLS for RADIUS clients: the NAS forwards EAP-Message attributes in Access-Requests, the daemon runs the TLS handshake with the EAP peer, maps the peer certificate to a configured user, and returns EAP-Success or EAP-Failure together with 802.1X keying material. EAP-TLS is the only supported EAP method; EAP-MD5, EAP-PEAP, and EAP-TTLS are not implemented, and EAP is never proxied or passed through to an external EAP server. This feature requires a build with OpenSSL support.

EAP is enabled per realm with an eap block; the block is accepted at top level (the default realm) and inside realm blocks, and follows the normal realm inheritance rules. A child realm disables EAP inherited from its parent with eap = no.

section.title: EAP-TLS Conversation and RFC 5216 Alignment
section.para: The EAP packet layer, fragmentation, identity handling, key derivation, and termination follow RFC 5216. In the base case the conversation is:
section.screen: NAS: EAP-Request/Identity peer: EAP-Response/Identity NAS: EAP-Request/EAP-TLS Start (S bit set, no data) peer: ClientHello server: TLS server flight peer: TLS client flight server: ChangeCipherSpec/Finished peer: empty EAP-Response/EAP-TLS NAS: EAP-Success
section.para: The server sends EAP-Success only after the peer's empty EAP-Response/EAP-TLS that acknowledges the server's final TLS flight; it does not send EAP-Success as soon as SSL_do_handshake() reports completion, because the peer has not yet received the server Finished message. When the final flight is fragmented, fragment ACKs are distinguished from the final completion ACK, and an empty response while more server fragments remain triggers the next fragment rather than EAP-Success.

EAP-TLS fragmentation follows RFC 5216 2.1.5. The L bit is set on the first fragment of a fragmented TLS message or set of messages and carries a 4-octet TLS Message Length; the M bit is set on all but the last fragment; the S bit appears only in the EAP-Request/EAP-TLS Start packet. The EAP Identifier is incremented for every fragment request and echoed by the peer in fragment ACKs; retransmitted fragments keep the same Identifier. A peer that receives a request with M set answers with an empty EAP-Response/EAP-TLS, and the server waits for that ACK before sending the next fragment. Reassembly is capped at the configured max-message (65535 bytes by default), matching RFC 5216's 64 KB guidance.

The peer identity is taken from the client certificate's subject CN or subjectAltName (RFC 5216 2.2 and 5.2), not from the EAP-Response/Identity. EAP-Response/Identity is unauthenticated and MUST NOT be used for access control, which is why eap-identity-source = eap-identity requires verify-client = no and is documented as lab-only. If the EAP-Response/Identity differs from the certificate identity, the certificate identity wins.

After a successful TLS 1.2 handshake the keying material is derived as Key_Material = TLS-PRF-128(master_secret, "client EAP encryption", client.random || server.random) (RFC 5216 2.3). The MSK is bytes 0 through 63 and the EMSK is bytes 64 through 127; MS-MPPE-Recv-Key is MSK[0..31] and MS-MPPE-Send-Key is MSK[32..63] (RFC 2548 2.4.2). OpenSSL's RFC 5705 exporter with an empty context produces the same TLS 1.2 PRF output.

Termination follows RFC 5216 2.1.3. On a peer authentication failure the server sends the TLS alert in an EAP-Request/EAP-TLS, waits for the peer's EAP-Response, and then sends EAP-Failure. If the peer reports a server-authentication failure (a TLS alert from the peer), the server sends EAP-Failure immediately. Restart-on-ClientHello is not implemented: any peer response after the alert is answered with EAP-Failure.

section.title: Deliberate Deviations from RFC 5216
section.para: The TLS profile deliberately deviates from RFC 5216 where the RFC is obsolete or conflicts with current security practice. This implementation therefore does not claim full RFC 5216 conformance:

listitem.para: TLS 1.2 is the only protocol version enabled. RFC 5216 requires TLS 1.0 support; TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are deprecated by RFC 8996 and disabled by modern OpenSSL security levels. TLS 1.3 and RFC 9190 key derivation are a follow-up.
3DES and RC4 ciphersuites are not enabled. RFC 5216 lists them, but they are deprecated by RFC 8996; the implementation uses OpenSSL's modern cipher defaults.
No TLS compression is negotiated (RFC 5216 2.4 requires no compression).

TLS session resumption, session tickets, renegotiation, and EAP fast reconnect are disabled, so the server flight is deterministic. EAP privacy (an empty EAP-Response/Identity and identity hiding) is out of scope.
Certificate revocation checking (CRL or OCSP) is out of scope (RFC 5216 5.4). A certificate is accepted when it chains to ca-file and passes the clientAuth purpose check.

section.title: EAP Packet Validation
section.para: The EAP header's Length field covers Code, Identifier, Length, Type, and Data. Octets outside the declared Length are data-link padding and are ignored on reception (RFC 5216 3.1 and 3.2). A packet with a declared length below 4, or above the number of bytes received in the concatenated EAP-Message attributes, is rejected.

Reserved bits are zero on send and ignored on receive. The S bit MUST NOT appear in an EAP-Response; a response that sets it is rejected. An EAP-Request from a NAS is treated as RADIUS role reversal (RFC 3579 2.6.2) and answered with an Access-Reject carrying EAP-Response/Nak proposing EAP-TLS. A Nak that proposes EAP-TLS causes the server to resend EAP-Request/EAP-TLS Start; a Nak proposing any other method fails the conversation.

Retransmissions are handled by a small reply cache keyed by the EAP Identifier, so a retransmitted Access-Request or fragment ACK receives the same reply without advancing the state machine. EAP-Success and EAP-Failure carry the Identifier of the client EAP-Response that triggered them.

section.title: Configuration
section.para: The eap block accepts the following directives:
section.screen: eap { eap-method = tls cert-file = $CONFDIR/democa/server-chain.pem key-file = $CONFDIR/democa/server.key ca-file = $CONFDIR/democa/root.crt verify-client = yes eap-identity-source = cert-cn timeout = 60 max-message = 65535 max-sessions = 4096 }

listitem.para: eap-method: tls is the only accepted value; other method names are a parse error.
cert-file: the EAP-TLS server certificate chain (PEM), required. key-file defaults to the same path when it is not set.
ca-file: the CA bundle used to verify the peer certificate, required when verify-client = yes.
passphrase: optional passphrase for an encrypted private key.
verify-client: yes by default. no is allowed only together with eap-identity-source = eap-identity, and is lab-only.

eap-identity-source: cert-cn (default), cert-san, or eap-identity. Certificate identities are lowercased before the user lookup; cert-san uses the first DNS subjectAltName and falls back to the CN when no DNS SAN exists.

timeout: seconds of inactivity before an EAP session/State entry expires; 60 by default and refreshed on every valid packet. The value must be at least 1 second; the usual s, m, h, and d suffixes are accepted. Explicit zero or negative values are parse errors.

max-message: hard cap for EAP-TLS reassembly in bytes, 65535 by default. The valid range is 4 through 65535, because the EAP Length field is 16-bit and the code needs room for the EAP-TLS header; explicit values outside that range are parse errors.

max-sessions: maximum number of concurrent EAP sessions per realm, 4096 by default. When the cap is reached, the session with the oldest activity is evicted. Must be positive; explicit zero or negative values are parse errors.

section.para: eap = no is also accepted as a realm-level directive so a child realm can disable EAP inherited from its parent. The broker-socket keyword does not exist in this phase; it is added with the UDP EAP broker.

section.title: Certificates and Identity Mapping
section.para: With verify-client = yes, the server requires a peer certificate (SSL_VERIFY_PEER | SSL_VERIFY_FAIL_IF_NO_PEER_CERT) and requires SSL_get_verify_result() to return X509_V_OK. The peer certificate must chain to ca-file and carry the clientAuth extended key usage, which OpenSSL enforces through X509_PURPOSE_SSL_CLIENT. Use a dedicated EAP-TLS server certificate and key rather than sharing the key with HTTPS or other services (RFC 5216 5.1).

Certificate-derived identities are converted to lower case (ASCII bytes) before the user lookup. Define the corresponding user names in lower case; there is no exact-match-then-lowercase fallback, because two lookup paths would create ambiguity. Embedded NUL bytes, empty identities, and identities longer than 255 bytes are rejected. With eap-identity-source = cert-san, the first GEN_DNS subjectAltName is used; if the certificate has no DNS SAN, the CN is used.

verify-client = no is only allowed with eap-identity-source = eap-identity, and any other combination is a parse error. In that mode the identity comes from the unauthenticated EAP-Response/Identity, so it must never be used for access control in a deployment that verifies certificates. A warning is logged at startup and for every authentication in that mode; it exists for lab testing only.

section.title: EAP-Message, State, and Message-Authenticator
section.para: EAP-Message is RADIUS attribute 79 and must be present in the RADIUS dictionary (the shipped radius-dict.cfg defines it). One RADIUS packet carries exactly one EAP packet, split across one or more consecutive EAP-Message attributes whose values are concatenated in order. Each attribute value is limited to 253 bytes. The NAS echoes the State attribute (24) from an Access-Challenge in its next Access-Request; State is limited to 16 bytes and is generated randomly by the server.

Every Access-Request, Access-Challenge, Access-Accept, and Access-Reject that contains EAP-Message carries a Message-Authenticator (80) on UDP and RADIUS/TCP. Over RadSec, an absent Message-Authenticator in an Access-Request is accepted because RFC 6614 relaxes RFC 3579; replies always include a Message-Authenticator. Message-Authenticator validation uses the RADIUS shared secret, including the static RadSec key where applicable.

RFC 3579 2.6.5 forbids Reply-Message in a packet that contains EAP-Message. Profile scripts can add attributes to the reply buffer, so the EAP reply path strips any Reply-Message already present from Access-Accept and Access-Reject. State belongs in Access-Challenge only, so Access-Accept and Access-Reject also omit State. If a profile fills the reply buffer so that EAP-Message plus Message-Authenticator no longer fit, the server falls back to a minimal Access-Reject containing EAP-Failure when that fits, and drops the reply otherwise.

section.title: Authorization, MFA, and Accounting Behavior
section.para: After the handshake completes, the certificate identity is mapped to a user and the request runs through the same host ACL, ruleset, user expiry, and profile evaluation as the password-based RADIUS path. Profile scripts can add RADIUS attributes to the Access-Accept, including Cisco-AVPair values. EAP-TLS authorization uses local user lookup only: it does not run MAVIS authentication and does not prefetch MAVIS information. A user whose login credential is MAVIS (password login = mavis) is rejected with EAP-Failure because MAVIS cannot be challenged inside EAP-TLS. Explicit login = deny and login = error credentials are also rejected; unlike the password paths, the EAP path does not send a RADIUS Protocol-Error, it sends EAP-Failure in an Access-Reject. A user with no login credential configured (the default deny placeholder) remains usable, because the verified client certificate is the credential for EAP-TLS.

MFA cannot be challenged inside EAP-TLS in this phase. If the selected host or user requires MFA, EAP authentication is rejected with EAP-Failure rather than silently bypassing the second factor. There is no option to disable this check.

The EAP path bypasses the RADIUS DACL check and the DNS reverse-mapping logic used by the password-based path. Downloadable ACLs (DACLs), CoA, and scripts that depend on nac_dns_name therefore see different behavior for EAP requests; if any of these becomes required for EAP, it needs a follow-up rather than a silent semantic change.

section.title: Fragmentation and Size Limits
section.para: RADIUS packets are limited to 4096 bytes, of which 20 bytes are the header, leaving at most 4076 bytes of attributes; the reply builder reserves 18 bytes for the Message-Authenticator. Server TLS output is split into EAP-TLS fragments of at most 3000 bytes (a safe default that leaves room for EAP-Message, State, and Message-Authenticator overhead), and each fragment is sent as an Access-Challenge with State. A RADIUS EAP-Message value is split into chunks of at most 253 bytes.

Client-to-server reassembly is bounded by max-message. The first fragment may announce the total TLS message length with the L bit; the announced total must be at least 1 and at most max-message. L on a non-first fragment, a first fragment with M but no L, and a reassembled length that does not match the announced total are rejected.

section.title: 802.1X Keying Attributes
section.para: After a successful handshake, an Access-Accept includes MS-MPPE-Recv-Key (vendor 311, type 17) and MS-MPPE-Send-Key (vendor 311, type 16), encrypted per RFC 2548 2.4.2 with the RADIUS shared secret and the current Request Authenticator. MS-MPPE-Encryption-Policy (311:7) defaults to 1 (Encryption-Allowed) and MS-MPPE-Encryption-Types (311:8) defaults to 6, matching the existing MSCHAP defaults. Keys are emitted only when a RADIUS secret is available; for RadSec that is the static "radsec" key. MSK and EMSK values are never logged and are zeroed before the EAP session is freed.
Access-Accept retransmissions re-encrypt the retained MSK halves with the new Request Authenticator instead of replaying cached ciphertext.

section.title: UDP, TCP, and TLS Transport Caveats
section.para: RADIUS/TCP and RADIUS/TLS have natural connection affinity, so EAP state stays in the worker handling the connection. RADIUS/UDP uses local per-worker EAP state in this phase. The daemon can be forced to a single process with spawnd single process = yes, but that setting is test-only and unsuitable for real life: it serializes all work and removes the availability the multi-worker design provides. Alternatively, sticky cache period can keep a NAS flow on one worker for a limited time, but it is not a guarantee: when the sticky entry expires or the assigned worker goes away, the flow can be dropped by that worker or moved to another one, and the EAP session table is per worker, so the conversation fails. Without either setting, consecutive Access-Requests of one EAP conversation can reach different workers, each with its own session table, and the conversation fails.

EAP sessions are not tac_session objects and are not counted in users_cur; the configured max-sessions limit applies per realm and per worker, not to the process-wide user count. There is no UDP EAP broker in this phase and no broker-socket keyword. The Phase 3 broker is the reliable multi-worker UDP path; until it exists, multi-worker UDP EAP should be avoided. EAP over DTLS is local-only as well. A SIGHUP causes spawnd to restart the daemon process; realms are re-read at startup, so in-flight EAP state is lost.

section.title: Unsupported Features
section.para: EAP-MD5, EAP-PEAP, and EAP-TTLS are not implemented, nor is RADIUS proxy or pass-through of EAP to an external server. EAP-TLS 1.3 and RFC 9190 key derivation are a follow-up. EAP privacy and fast reconnect are out of scope, as are CRL and OCSP certificate revocation checks. TACACS+ has no standard EAP extension (RFC 8907 does not define one), so EAP is RADIUS-only.

para.emphasis: I'm using the single-connection feature. How can I force my router to close the TCP connections to the TACACS+ server?

listitem.para: On IOS, show tcp brief will display the TCP connections. Search for the ones terminating at your server, and kill them using clear tcp tcb .... Example:
listitem.screen: Router#sho tcp brief | incl 10.0.0.1.49 633BB794 10.0.0.2.17326 10.0.0.1.49 ESTAB 6287E4C4 10.0.0.2.24880 10.0.0.1.49 ESTAB Router#clear tcp tcb 633BB794 [confirm] [OK] Router#clear tcp tcb 6287E4C4 [confirm] [OK] Router#

para.emphasis: Is there any way to avoid having clear text versions of the CHAP secrets in the configuration file?

listitem.para: CHAP requires that the server knows the cleartext password (or equivalently, something from which the server can generate the cleartext password). Note that this is part of the definition of CHAP, not just the whim of some Cisco engineer who drank too much coffee late one night.

If we encrypted the CHAP passwords in the database, then we'd need to keep a key around so that the server can decrypt them when CHAP needs them. So this only ends up being a slight obfuscation and not much more secure than the original scheme.

In extended TACACS, the CHAP secrets were separated from the password file because the password file may be a system password file and hence world readable. But with TACACS+'s native database, there is no such requirement, so we think the best solution is to read-protect the files. Note that this is the same problem that a Kerberos server has. If your security is compromised on the Kerberos server, then your database is wide open. Kerberos does encrypt the database, but if you want your server to automatically restart, then you end up having to "kstash" the key in a file anyway and you're back to the same security problem.
So storing the cleartext password on the security server is really an absolute requirement of the CHAP protocols, not something imposed by TACACS+.

With the scheme choosen for newer TACACS+ protocol revisions, the NAS sends the challenge information to the TACACS+ daemon and the daemon uses the cleartext password to generate the response and returns that.

The original TACACS+ protocol included specific protocol knowledge for CHAP. Please note that this version of the daemon implementation no longer supports SENDPASS, SENDAUTH and ARAP to comply to RFC8907.
However, the above doesn't apply to PAP. You can keep an inbound PAP password DES- or MD5-encrypted, since all you need to do with it is verify that the password the principal gave you is correct.

para.emphasis: How is the typical login authentication sequence done?

listitem.para: NAS sends START packet to daemon
Daemon send GETUSER containing login prompt to NAS
NAS prompts user for username
NAS sends packet to daemon
Daemon sends GETPASS containing password prompt to the NAS
NAS prompts user for password
NAS sends packet to daemon
Daemon sends accept, reject or error to NAS

para.emphasis: How can I configure time-outs on an interface via TACACS+?

listitem.para: Certain per-user/per-interface timeouts may be set by TACACS+ during authorization. As of 11.0, you can set an exec timeout. As of 11.1 you can also set an exec idle timeout.

There are currently no settable timeouts for PPP or SLIP sessions, but there is a workaround which applies to ASYNC PPP/SLIP idle timeouts started via exec sessions only: This workaround is to set an EXEC (idletime) timeout on an exec session which is later used to start up PPP or SLIP (either via a TACACS+ autocommand or via the user explicitly invoking PPP or SLIP). In this case, the exec idle timeout will correctly terminate an idle PPP or SLIP session. Note that this workaround cannot be used for sessions which autoselect PPP or SLIP.

An idle timeout terminates a connection when the interface is idle for a given period of time (this is equivalent to the "session-timeout" Cisco IOS configuration directive). The other timeouts are absolute. Of course, any timeouts set by TACACS+ apply only to the current connection.
You also need to configure exec authorization on the NAS for the above timeouts, e.g.
listitem.screen: aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+
listitem.para: Note that these timeouts only work for async lines, not for ISDN currently.
Note also that you cannot use the authorization if-authenticated option with these parameters, since that skips authorization if the user has successfully authenticated.

para.emphasis: Can someone expand on the use of the optional keyword?

listitem.para: Most attributes are mandatory i.e. if the daemon sends them to the NAS, the NAS must obey them or deny the authorization. This is the default. It is possible to mark attributes as optional, in which case a NAS which cannot support the attribute is free to simply ignore it without causing the authorization to fail.

This was intended to be useful in cutover situations where you have multiple NASes running different versions of IOS, some of which support more attributes than others. If you make the new attributes optional, older NASes could ignore the optional attributes while new NASes could apply them. Note that this weakens your security a little, since you are no longer guaranteed that attributes are always applied on successful authorization, so it should be used judiciously.
The daemon comes with mschap support. Mschap is configured the same way as chap, only using the mschap keyword in place of the chap keyword.
MSCHAP requires DES support. Use the --with-ssl flag when configuring the package.
Marc Huber thinks that MSCHAP relevance is less than zero and expects it to be removed from the standard, as nobody uses it anyway.

section.title: AAA rule tracing
section.para: The distribution includes the tactrace.pl Perl script. It's usually not installed automatically, due to some Perl dependencies that need to be met. It requires a couple of CPAN Perl modules, and a custom one. Your OS distribution might provide re-built packages for Net::IP and/or Net::TacacsPlus::Packet, so check for this first. For unavailable packages, you can do a manual install using cpan. Example for Ubuntu:
section.screen: sudo apt install libnet-ip-perl sudo cpan install Net::TacacsPlus::Packet
section.para: Then cd to tac_plus-ng/perl and run make. tactrace.pl should now be ready to use.
